quests.instruction: Select the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: It's about food, but not about eating.
quests.explanation: 'Piece of cake' describes a task that takes almost no effort. "Don't stress about the driving test — after all that practice, it'll be a piece of cake."
quests.origin: Recorded in American English since the 1930s; the exact reason cake was chosen as the symbol of 'easy' isn't documented, though cake was already linked to something pleasant and effortless to enjoy.

quests.instruction: I caught a cold and had to skip the party because I was feeling ___.
quests.hint: Think about how sailors used to describe seasickness.
quests.explanation: 'Under the weather' means mildly ill. "I'm a bit under the weather today, so I might leave the meeting early."
quests.origin: Believed to come from sailing: a sick crew member was sent below deck, 'under the weather rail,' away from the storm — though the full nautical story is hard to confirm precisely.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Go to bed for the night.
quests.explanation: 'Hit the sack' simply means to go to bed. "It's almost midnight — I should hit the sack before my flight."
quests.origin: Dates to early 1900s slang, when cheap mattresses were literally cloth sacks stuffed with straw or feathers.

quests.instruction: Which idiom fits this situation?
quests.hint: A phrase performers say to each other right before a show.
quests.explanation: 'Break a leg' is a way of wishing a performer good luck. "Break a leg out there tonight — the whole cast has worked so hard."
quests.origin: A well-known theatre superstition holds that wishing someone 'good luck' directly would jinx them, so performers said the opposite instead. The exact origin remains debated among theatre historians.

quests.instruction: We only get snow here ___, so the kids were thrilled.
quests.hint: It's about how rarely something happens, not about color.
options: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.explanation: 'Once in a blue moon' describes something that happens very rarely. "He visits his hometown once in a blue moon, maybe once every few years."
quests.origin: A 'blue moon' refers to a second full moon in one calendar month, an astronomical event that happens only occasionally — which is why it became shorthand for rarity.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Having the same understanding or opinion as someone else.
options: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.explanation: 'On the same page' means everyone shares the same understanding. "Before we launch, let's make sure the whole team is on the same page about the timeline."
quests.origin: A straightforward metaphor from reading: people literally looking at the same page of a document are following along together.

quests.word: COST AN ARM AND A LEG
quests.instruction: The new laptop looked great, but it cost ___.
quests.hint: It describes a price, and it isn't a compliment.
options: COST AN ARM AND A LEG
quests.explanation: 'Cost an arm and a leg' means something is extremely expensive. "Renting downtown costs an arm and a leg these days."
quests.correctAnswer: COST AN ARM AND A LEG
quests.origin: First appeared in American English in the mid-20th century. A popular story links it to portrait painting, but there's no solid evidence for that — the true origin is uncertain.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Reveal secret information, often by accident.
quests.explanation: 'Spill the beans' means to give away a secret. "Please don't spill the beans about the surprise party!"
quests.origin: In use in American English since the early 1900s; an older theory connects it to ancient Greek voting with beans, but that link isn't well supported by evidence.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Leave and begin a journey.
options: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.explanation: 'Hit the road' means to set off on a trip or leave a place. "It's getting late — we should hit the road if we want to beat traffic."
quests.origin: Emerged in American English in the early 20th century, using 'hit' in the informal sense of 'reach' or 'set out on.'

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Do or say something to ease tension in an awkward social moment.
quests.explanation: 'Break the ice' means to relieve awkwardness, especially when people first meet. "The host asked everyone to share a fun fact to break the ice."
quests.origin: Refers to ships historically called 'icebreakers,' which cut a path through frozen water so other ships could follow — the phrase extended to 'clearing a path' in conversation.

quests.instruction: I sat down to answer one email, and suddenly it was 6 p.m. — ___!
quests.hint: It's a comment people make when they're surprised by how much time has passed.
options: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.explanation: 'Time flies' is said when time seems to pass unexpectedly fast. "Time flies when you're having fun — I can't believe the trip is already over."
quests.origin: A shortened form of the Latin phrase 'tempus fugit,' which has been quoted in English since at least the 16th century.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Lose an opportunity by acting too late.
quests.explanation: 'Miss the boat' means to fail to take advantage of a chance in time. "Early bird tickets sold out — I guess we missed the boat on that discount."
quests.origin: A literal image turned figurative: someone who arrives at the dock after a ship has already left has, quite simply, missed it.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Force yourself to do something unpleasant that can't be avoided.
quests.explanation: 'Bite the bullet' means to accept a difficult or painful situation and get on with it. "I hate calling customer service, but I'll just bite the bullet and get it done."
quests.origin: Traditionally linked to battlefield surgery before anesthesia, when a wounded soldier supposedly bit down on a bullet to endure the pain — a vivid story, though historians note the evidence for it is thin.

quests.instruction: Can I ___ on dinner tonight? I'm exhausted, but I'd love to reschedule.
quests.hint: It's a polite way to say 'not now, but maybe later.'
options: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.explanation: 'Take a rain check' means to postpone an invitation to a later time. "Take a rain check on coffee — how about Thursday instead?"
quests.origin: Comes from baseball: if a game was rained out, ticket holders received a 'rain check' voucher to attend a future game.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Become nervous and hesitant about a plan right before doing it.
quests.explanation: 'Get cold feet' means to lose your nerve at the last moment, often before a big decision. "He almost backed out of the wedding speech — total cold feet."
quests.origin: Recorded in English since the late 1800s; the image of feet literally going cold from fear or hesitation made the phrase easy to adopt figuratively.

quests.instruction: We were just talking about Maya, and then she walked in — ___!
quests.hint: Said when someone appears right after being mentioned.
quests.explanation: 'Speak of the devil' is said when a person shows up right after being mentioned in conversation. "Speak of the devil — we were just talking about your new job!"
quests.origin: Shortened from an older superstition, 'speak of the devil and he shall appear,' warning that naming something dangerous might summon it.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Keep trying and don't give up, even when things are hard.
options: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.explanation: 'Hang in there' is used to encourage someone going through a tough time. "I know finals are stressful — just hang in there, you're almost done."
quests.origin: Popularized in the mid-1900s and famously paired with a poster of a cat clinging to a branch, though the phrase itself predates that image.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Reach a final decision after considering the options.
quests.explanation: 'Make up your mind' means to finally decide. "You've looked at ten apartments — it's time to make up your mind."
quests.origin: A straightforward extension of 'mind' as something that can be mentally arranged or settled, in use since at least the 16th century.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Decide to stop working on something for now.
quests.explanation: 'Call it a day' means to stop an activity, usually because enough has been done. "We've painted three rooms already — let's call it a day."
quests.origin: Originated in early 20th-century American English from the earlier phrase 'call it half a day,' referring to workers stopping early.

quests.instruction: Could you ___ the soup while I answer the door? I don't want it to boil over.
quests.hint: It means to watch something carefully so nothing goes wrong.
options: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.explanation: 'Keep an eye on' means to watch or monitor something closely. "Can you keep an eye on my bag while I grab a coffee?"
quests.origin: A literal-sounding phrase that became fixed through everyday use — the eye stands in for attention and supervision.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Forced to start over from the very beginning.
quests.explanation: 'Back to square one' means returning to the starting point after a setback. "The client rejected the whole design, so we're back to square one."
quests.origin: Often linked to early board games or radio football commentary that divided a pitch into numbered squares, though the precise source is debated.

quests.word: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Tell someone firmly and angrily what you think of their behavior.
options: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.explanation: 'Give someone a piece of your mind' means to express strong criticism or anger directly to someone. "After the third late delivery, she called the company to give them a piece of her mind."
quests.correctAnswer: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.origin: In use since the 1500s, treating opinions as something that can literally be handed over, piece by piece.

quests.instruction: We had a great plan for the presentation, but we ___ before finishing the last slide.
quests.hint: It means there wasn't enough time left to finish.
quests.explanation: 'Run out of time' means the available time is used up before something is complete. "We ran out of time during the interview and never got to my questions."
quests.origin: A plain, transparent extension of 'run out of' (a supply), applied to time as something that can be used up.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Set money aside now in case it's needed during hard times later.
options: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.explanation: 'Save for a rainy day' means to keep money in reserve for future trouble. "He puts a little from every paycheck aside, just to save for a rainy day."
quests.origin: Uses 'rainy day' as a symbol of hard or gloomy times, a metaphor for misfortune found in English since at least the 1500s.

quests.word: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Describe or identify something exactly and accurately.
options: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.explanation: 'Hit the nail on the head' means to be exactly right about something. "You hit the nail on the head — the real problem was poor communication, not the budget."
quests.correctAnswer: HIT THE NAIL ON THE HEAD
quests.origin: A carpentry image: striking a nail precisely on its head drives it in cleanly, unlike a glancing, inaccurate hit.

quests.instruction: After the surgery, the doctor told him to ___ for a couple of weeks.
quests.hint: It's advice to relax and avoid stress or overexertion.
quests.explanation: 'Take it easy' means to relax or not push yourself too hard. "You've been working nonstop — take it easy this weekend."
quests.origin: A simple, long-established use of 'easy' as a state to move into, dating back to informal English of the 1800s.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Facing the same difficult situation as someone else.
quests.explanation: 'In the same boat' means sharing the same problem or circumstances as others. "Don't worry, half the class failed that quiz — we're all in the same boat."
quests.origin: A nautical metaphor: people literally sharing one boat share the same fate if it sinks or survives.

quests.instruction: Select the idiom with this meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Happening suddenly and without any warning.
quests.explanation: 'Out of the blue' describes something completely unexpected. "He called me out of the blue after five years of silence."
quests.origin: Likely shortened from 'a bolt out of the blue,' comparing a sudden surprise to lightning striking from a clear sky.

quests.instruction: She was in tears before the interview, but she knew she had to ___ before walking in.
quests.hint: It means to regain control of your emotions.
options: GIVE SOMEONE A PIECE OF YOUR MIND
quests.explanation: 'Pull yourself together' means to calm down and regain composure, especially after being upset. "Take a breath and pull yourself together — you've got this."
quests.origin: In use since the 19th century, imagining scattered emotions as pieces that need to be gathered back into order.

quests.instruction: Choose the idiom that matches the meaning.
quests.hint: DEFINITION: Something that sounds simple to suggest but is actually hard to do.
quests.explanation: 'Easier said than done' points out that an idea is harder to carry out in practice than it is to talk about. "'Just relax,' she said. Easier said than done when your flight leaves in ten minutes."
quests.origin: A centuries-old English proverb, recorded in similar form since at least the 1300s, contrasting speech with action.
